item.title: Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
item.description: Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. In this post, we preview data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Rohlf

Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability.

Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. With these results in mind, we discuss how developers can apply similar techniques to their own code.

Methods for reducing codebases’ attack surface

Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another. This can often cause it to function very differently to how its original developers intended. And it is a big part of why attackers are often so successful: they study exactly how a piece of code behaves in practice, rather than how its developers intended or designed it to work.

Automated attack surface analysis and reduction techniques aim to discover unnecessary attack surfaces, then move that code behind an appropriate gate. This might involve moving code from pre-authentication to post-authentication, from 0-click to 1-click, from on-by-default to explicit opt-in, or from the first message of a protocol to deeper in the session state machine. Some code is meant to be reachable before these stages, but a lot it is not, and, given the complexity that comes with code churn across thousands or millions of lines of code, unnecessary exposure of features often goes unnoticed.

There are numerous ways to reduce the attack surface of code. In our own research efforts, we focused on three methods in particular:

  • Default configuration. We identified code that was reachable in its shipped default configuration but wasn’t intended to be used by any default functionality.
  • Configuration interaction. We found pairs of options that looked reasonable on their own, but which caused issues when configured together (for instance, by silently disabling a security control, or leaving a features behavior undefined while its code remains reachable).
  • Early reachability. We identified security sensitive and complex code that runs either before an appropriate security control (such as authentication), without victim interaction, or before a protocol state transition.

We wanted to understand how well Claude could take these three descriptions of attack surface and discover real issues in large and complex codebases. We analyzed 25 open source projects (representing over five million lines of code), written in languages including C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python. Claude created an inventory of over 17,000 configuration options across these projects. Of those, 3,842 related to the configuration of a control or feature that was security relevant.

For the purposes of our research, we broke down these open source projects into three broad categories:

  • Public. These projects are built to serve any user who can reach them, or to consume data authored by parties they cannot identify. (Examples include a DNS resolver parsing upstream answers, or a proxy parsing origin responses.)
  • Gated. These projects are intended to serve authenticated users (such as those with a password, key or certificate holders, or enrolled devices). The software still allows for arbitrary client requests, but no functionality is available until the user has been authenticated.
  • Private. These are built and deployed to serve the operator's own private environment. In these cases, adding a control like an authentication layer is optional, but outside the scope of the software.

These categories help to contextualize our results. For example, we’d expect a significant percentage of a Public codebase to be reachable in the default configuration (since it’s designed to serve any user), but the opposite to be true for projects in the Gated category.

Claude’s findings

Claude found 493 issues using the three methods described above. Several themes stuck out to us from its results.

First, Claude found that all eleven gated projects had code that was unintentionally reachable (although this code wasn’t a significant percentage of the total lines of code for any of those projects). Specifically, Claude discovered 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces in the default configuration of the gated cohort, 37 locations where code executed, or state was recorded, before authentication, and 61 configuration combinations that silently weakened a pre-authentication control configured by the administrator. None of these issues would have been immediately exploitable on their own, but they create a much larger attack surface than is necessary.

Second, Claude’s work mitigating configuration interaction issues produced some of the most interesting and impactful findings (across all project types). Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction. In 94 of those cases, the combination silently turned off a security control. The other 68 cases were inconsistencies in the same security mechanisms (e.g. a listener or login path would remain reachable even though the configuration would say it was disabled; two settings would conflict, and the one that would take precedence would depend on their order in the configuration file, or a protection configured by the administrator would do nothing while its code remained reachable). While some of these configuration combinations might be non-standard or infrequently used, there would be nothing preventing an administrator of these projects from configuring and deploying the code in this way.

Claude also found one specific pattern that turned up independently in four unrelated projects. This would work as follows. An administrator would write an access rule for remote clients using a hostname or a wildcard pattern, instead of an IP address. When a client connects, the server would compare that rule against the client’s hostname. Whether the server ever learned that hostname would depend on a separate option that controlled reverse DNS lookups (which most projects had configured off). With lookups off, the server would only have the client’s IP address. The server would compare the rule against that address as plain text. But a hostname pattern can never match an IP address. This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open. Some of the affected projects mention in their documentation that hostname rules depend on DNS lookups being enabled, but none state that a deny list written this way would have fail open behavior.

Third, Claude often discovered that two configuration options would conflict in a way that silently dropped a security check. In one case, an administrator could require every connecting client to prove its identity with a certificate. In another, the code was only intended to delay that check until it was required, but in fact disabled the check entirely. A server that was configured to accept only trusted clients would therefore accept a connection from anyone. This exposed a large body of request handling code (which was supposed to be behind the certificate check) to unauthenticated clients. The software accepted both configuration options together with no warning under default settings; the documentation never mentioned that the certificate requirement had been dropped. This conflicting set of configuration options had been present in the software for 21 years.

Finally, Claude discovered an issue in a project that left authentication off by default (and expected the administrator to turn it on). The option that required TLS client certificates was honored on most of the project’s network endpoints, but silently ignored on a few others (ones which loaded their TLS settings through a path with a different namespace). This meant that a client with no certificate could complete the TLS handshake and open a session on an affected endpoint. Nothing would be logged about the ignored setting. Whether the option takes effect would depend on the namespace used by the administrator in the configuration. One form of the setting name works on every endpoint, but the shorter form—which most examples use—is dropped on the affected ones.

Case study: OpenSSH

Surprisingly, when measured as a percentage of the total lines of code, the project for which Claude achieved the largest reduction in attack surface was OpenSSH. OpenSSH is a high quality C codebase that provides secure remote access. Claude traced the input paths of the SSH daemon in the 10.4 release and found roughly 4,500 lines of new and experimental code for ML-DSA-44, a post-quantum signature algorithm, that an unauthenticated client could reach in the default configuration. ML-DSA is not enabled by default, but the code was reachable regardless, even when an administrator explicitly excluded the algorithm. The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed. There is no good reason for this complex, memory unsafe code to be reachable when it hasn’t been enabled by the configuration. Those 4,500 lines of code in ML-DSA-44 are about 16% of OpenSSH’s own pre-authentication code in a default sshd. We reported this to the OpenSSH developers along with patches. The 10.5 release moved the check before parsing.

Claude then noted two gaps in the 10.5 check. The first was a mismatch between what the client claimed and what it sent. The check looked at the algorithm name advertised by the client, but the parser was chosen by a type string embedded inside the key blob. A client could advertise ssh-ed25519, pass the check, and still send an ML-DSA key that would be parsed.

The second gap was in the 10.5 check’s certificates. Certificate key types were enabled by default. Given a certificate supplied by an attacker, sshd would deserialize the embedded CA public key and run a full signature verification with it, for any supported algorithm, before consulting the configuration. The user key signature path was properly gated behind the list of public keys allowed to connect to the server, but the CA signature path was not. That made every public key signature verifier in the binary reachable by any client that could complete a key exchange. We built a proof of concept and worked through several iterations of a fix with the maintainers. The resulting change placed the checks inside the parser itself. The encoded key type and the certificate’s CA signature algorithm are now compared against the configured allow lists before the corresponding deserialization or signature verification.

This fix removed roughly a fifth of the OpenSSH code that an unauthenticated client previously could have reached in a default build. Almost all of that was the new ML-DSA code, which is now unreachable even for a client that lies about its key type or hides an ML-DSA CA key inside an otherwise acceptable certificate. Certificates signed with an allowed CA algorithm are still parsed and verified, but the check now runs before parsing. The maintainers shipped the changes described here in version 10.6.

OpenSSH is some of the most heavily audited code in the world. If unnecessary reachability survives there, it can survive anywhere. This suggests that reducing the attack surface of codebases is likely to pay dividends across many important codebases.

Conclusion

It is perhaps impossible to measure how many unknown vulnerabilities are in any given codebase. And there is plenty of data that shows attackers can and will find those vulnerabilities with enough time (particularly if equipped with frontier AI models). But a defender who reduces unnecessary attack surface in their code reduces the risk from all of the unknown vulnerabilities in that code at once—including any that are already being quietly exploited. OpenSSH is some of the most audited C code in the world. Yet it shipped around 4,500 lines of experimental signature parsing code that could have been reached by an attacker prior to any configuration check.

We have combined the attack surface reduction techniques we described above into one reusable Claude skill, which we are working to integrate into OSS-Scanner. The skill runs three passes on a codebase. Each time it starts fresh (with an empty context window), except for a short piece of context it receives from the prior pass.

In the first pass, the skill looks at whether there is code that the default configuration allows to be reached but which isn’t used by any intended functionality. In the second pass, it looks at the code that runs before any hard gates (like authentication) or before protocol state machine entry points, in any configuration. Finally, third, the skill assesses which combinations of configurations silently switch a security control off or degrade its efficacy. In every pass, Claude creates an inventory of the entry points from the code and confirms each finding with a dynamic trace of the program. For default configuration findings, it designs and implements a gate and ensures that this causes no change in the program’s default behavior. It does so by running the project's own test suite (along with a black box regression suite) against the baseline; it requires modified builds to have identical results. Any gate that would change a non-default configuration is set aside for a human to decide. For the other two passes, it proposes changes like reordering a configuration check, adding a guard to enforce state ordering, or rejecting the combination at configuration load. Even without using this specific skill, we think the broad methodology outlined here is likely to be effective.

The techniques outlined in this post offer only a very limited view into what is possible in attack surface reduction. For instance, Claude is also capable of analyzing and comparing runtime logs against configurations to ensure that only required functionality has been enabled: disabling unused parsers, legacy protocols, and dashboards reduces security risk at little cost.

We encourage organizations to explore using Claude to analyze and reduce the attack surface of the software they depend on. We expect this to be one of the most practical ways that developers can measurably improve the security of the code the world already runs on.

item.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
item.description: The decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.
item.content:encoded:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”
Jerry Solinas, 2015

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Claude found the seeds

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

What this means

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

How it was found

Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.

Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:

This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.
Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.

Claude found some base points too

But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?

While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.

The recipe here is simple:

  1. Seed the generator with a small integer.
  2. Throw away seven outputs.
  3. Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
  4. Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.

Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.

As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.

Open questions

Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.

The bounty

The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.

Who we are

This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.

Acknowledgements

We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.

Code to reproduce the seeds

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def unix(when):
    return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())

def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width):
    x, out = (t << 16) | 0x330E, ""                      # the state srand48(t) sets
    for i in range(per * n):
        x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48              # one step of lrand48
        if i >= per * (n - 1):
            out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift)
    return out

PRIME = {  # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23
    "prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185),
    "prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320),
    "prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048),
    "P-192":      ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 139),
    "prime192v3": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 5228),
    "prime192v2": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 6013),
    "P-521":      ("1997-08-08 01:12:04", 1136),
    "P-256":      ("1997-08-16 01:52:34", 1842),
    "P-384":      ("1997-08-30 14:50:08", 2688),
    "P-224":      ("1998-04-03 12:52:07", 7026),
}
BINARY = {  # srand48(time / 2), if that reading is right; 5 words per candidate: lrand48()
    "B-233": ("1998-04-17 15:24:18", 155),
    "B-283": ("1998-04-17 15:27:44", 32),
    "B-409": ("1998-04-17 15:30:18", 60),
    "B-571": ("1998-04-17 15:32:08", 73),
}
for name, (when, n) in PRIME.items():
    print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when), n, 20, 40, 2)}")
for name, (when, n) in BINARY.items():
    print(f"{name:10} {when} {n:5} {candidate(unix(when) // 2, n, 5, 17, 8)}")

The output of this code:

prime239v1 1997-05-15 15:49:03  2185 E43BB460F0B80CC0C0B075798E948060F8321B7D
prime239v2 1997-05-15 15:49:03  2320 E8B4011604095303CA3B8099982BE09FCB9AE616
prime239v3 1997-05-15 15:49:03  3048 7D7374168FFE3471B60A857686A19475D3BFA2FF
P-192      1997-05-18 14:45:34   139 3045AE6FC8422F64ED579528D38120EAE12196D5
prime192v3 1997-05-18 14:45:34  5228 C469684435DEB378C4B65CA9591E2A5763059A2E
prime192v2 1997-05-18 14:45:34  6013 31A92EE2029FD10D901B113E990710F0D21AC6B6
P-521      1997-08-08 01:12:04  1136 D09E8800291CB85396CC6717393284AAA0DA64BA
P-256      1997-08-16 01:52:34  1842 C49D360886E704936A6678E1139D26B7819F7E90
P-384      1997-08-30 14:50:08  2688 A335926AA319A27A1D00896A6773A4827ACDAC73
P-224      1998-04-03 12:52:07  7026 BD71344799D5C7FCDC45B59FA3B9AB8F6A948BC5
B-233      1998-04-17 15:24:18   155 74D59FF07F6B413D0EA14B344B20A2DB049B50C3
B-283      1998-04-17 15:27:44    32 77E2B07370EB0F832A6DD5B62DFC88CD06BB84BE
B-409      1998-04-17 15:30:18    60 4099B5A457F9D69F79213D094C4BCD4D4262210B
B-571      1998-04-17 15:32:08    73 2AA058F73A0E33AB486B0F610410C53A7F132310

Code to reproduce selected base points

M, A = 2**107 - 1, pow(3, 121, 2**107 - 1)       # zrandom: state = state * 3^121 mod (2^107 - 1)
P192 = 2**192 - 2**64 - 1
P239 = 2**239 - 2**143 - 2**95 + 2**47 - 1

CURVES = [  # name, LIP seed, p, b, published Gx   (a = -3 throughout)
    ("prime192v1", 20000, P192,
     0x64210519e59c80e70fa7e9ab72243049feb8deecc146b9b1,
     0x188da80eb03090f67cbf20eb43a18800f4ff0afd82ff1012),
    ("prime239v1", 20420, P239,
     0x6b016c3bdcf18941d0d654921475ca71a9db2fb27d1d37796185c2942c0a,
     0xffa963cdca8816ccc33b8642bedf905c3d358573d3f27fbbd3b3cb9aaaf),
    ("prime239v2", 20507, P239,
     0x617fab6832576cbbfed50d99f0249c3fee58b94ba0038c7ae84c8c832f2c,
     0x38af09d98727705120c921bb5e9e26296a3cdcf2f35757a0eafd87b830e7),
    ("prime239v3", 20509, P239,
     0x255705fa2a306654b1f4cb03d6a750a30c250102d4988717d9ba15ab6d3e,
     0x6768ae8e18bb92cfcf005c949aa2c6d94853d0e660bbf854b1c9505fe95a),
    ("prime192v2", 20512, P192,
     0xcc22d6dfb95c6b25e49c0d6364a4e5980c393aa21668d953,
     0xeea2bae7e1497842f2de7769cfe9c989c072ad696f48034a),
    ("prime192v3", 20517, P192,
     0x22123dc2395a05caa7423daeccc94760a7d462256bd56916,
     0x7d29778100c65a1da1783716588dce2b8b4aee8e228f1896),
]

def base_point_x(seed, p, b):
    state = seed                         # zrstarts(seed)
    def limb():                          # zrandom(2^26): low 26 bits of the new state
        nonlocal state
        state = state * A % M
        return state % 2**26
    for _ in range(7):                   # seven single-limb draws come first
        limb()
    limbs = -(-p.bit_length() // 26) + 1 # zrandomb(p): limbs of p plus one, top limb first
    tries = 0
    while True:
        x = 0
        for _ in range(limbs):
            x = x << 26 | limb()
        x %= p
        tries += 1
        if pow(x**3 - 3*x + b, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1:   # is x on the curve?
            return x, tries

for name, seed, p, b, gx in CURVES:
    x, tries = base_point_x(seed, p, b)

item.title: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter
item.description: Small AI models may be only months away from being able to self-replicate across cheap IoT devices like Android TV boxes, with no datacenter needed.
item.content:encoded:
William Zhou, Daniel Freeman

Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial IoT devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off - though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evals, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end. In our simplified evals, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year. Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.

Introduction

Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control.

In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. Prior work has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.

Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model.

We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs.

Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps.

We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here.

In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators.

Threat modelling

In this blog post, we’re focused on one way that AI worms might propagate: small models that replicate through compromising their host machines. But there are several other methods that AI worms might try: they could steal access in order to spin up hosts (for example, API keys or platform credentials) or pay for inference through legitimate work (e.g digital freelancing). The threat models that we think are closest to being realized today are the following:

  1. A small model, replicating via host compromise. In this post, we’ll call autonomous worms that run their models directly on compromised hardware weight-based replicators. Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place.

    A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well.
    1. Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve.
  2. A large, advanced weight-based replicator focused on datacenters and other high-compute targets. Larger models tend to have correspondingly better cyber capabilities, but will also need to breach (relatively) hardened datacenters to run themselves. We split this threat model into two subcategories:
    1. Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up unmonitored internal deployments or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute.
    2. Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored.
  3. An API-based replicator, in which a model would replicate by stealing credentials for their own inference API. These replicators would require a model provider to unknowingly serve them, and their persistence may be worse, since they’d likely be easier to discover (although their rate of spread may be higher, if for instance they’re able to replicate using victims’ accounts).

In practice, an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic ‘worst case scenario’ attack.

In this blog post, we consider the feasibility of small weight-based replicators (section 1 of the above). We focus on this because it’s a near-term threat model that can be investigated directly. Our demo at the top of this post, a 26B model running across 15 boxes, shows that IoT devices can run surprisingly capable models. Could these models be capable enough to carry out autonomous replication?

We examine this in two parts. First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run?

A. Inference setup

Of the stages in the above diagram showing the replication cycle, inference setup is the least studied and may be the most challenging for small models. It requires a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.

Evaluating inference setup performance

We measure the ability of different open-weight models to serve Llama3.1-8B across heterogeneous hardware types. See the table below for tokens per second served across various hardware types:

  • Click a cell for its distribution of serving speeds.
  • Click a row/column label to get a comparison across models or hardware type.

Small models, such as Qwen3.5-9B, are capable of setting up inference servers on hardware from Jetson Nanos to Mac PCs and RTX 4090s. More capable models such as GLM-5.2 are not only more reliable but also achieve higher serve tokens/s, allowing for faster replication. We test and mention specific chips to measure how well models can set up inference on them. The chips aren’t a source of risk or vulnerabilities.

We run these experiments using Memento, a harness we built on top of the open-source Pi coding agent. Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API.

Memento periodically starts a fresh agent instance with the previous agent’s workspace and a short set of notes written by the previous agent on what it tried, allowing later instances to pursue different strategies.

How does a model run on Smart TVs?

IoT devices are light on memory, but distributed inference as in Petals makes serving our lightweight models feasible. The representative threat model is Kimwolf, a large IoT botnet that infected over two million devices, primarily off-brand Android TVs. Such smart TV boxes, which are readily available for purchase, typically run forks of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which their manufacturers don’t add security features to. Typical boxes in this range ship with between 1 and 4 gigabytes of RAM. Assuming 4GB of RAM at 4-bit quantization, this allows for inference of 9B models with 4 or more machines, and inference of 26B models with 10+ machines.

In the demo at the top of this post, we ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 smart TV boxes with 4GB of RAM each. We sharded the model under pipeline parallelism, where each box holds a small fraction of the model’s layers.

B. Going viral: autonomous setup and replication across a GCP node fleet

Now that we’ve seen that models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, let’s measure whether models are capable of composing the steps—that is, scanning a network for targets, accessing them via a reverse shell, sending over the viral payload (weights and harness), and setting up inference.

Autonomous inference setup and replication (with simplified cyber)

To do this, we built a firewalled VPC of 8 GCP nodes running redroid, an Android 15 emulator. Patient zero (gray node) is seeded with the worm. Every subsequent infection is the worm itself hopping node to node over an unauthenticated ADB port, before setting up an inference server to serve Llama3.1-8B. If the inference server passes a number of correctness and anti-cheating checks, we spawn another copy of the worm on the target node (for example, if GLM-5.2 sets up Llama3.1 to run on a machine, we spawn a copy of the GLM-5.2 worm on it). The worm’s model runs on a separate inference server, since the VPC nodes aren’t large enough to run the larger models.

In the graph below, we drop a given model in as a payload and measure its ability to replicate.

Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication (assuming its capabilities could be packed into Llama3.1-8B). Note that GLM-5.2 does this reliably while the other models fail reliably (it spread to 8/8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials and 7/8 in 1).

It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process. Our evaluation keeps the cyber-exploit element of the replication trivial (there’s no authentication over the ADB port), which makes this an upper bound on real-world success. Note that past IoT botnets have replicated via means as simple as going through a default list of manufacturer usernames and passwords, as in the case of the Mirai botnet, so real IoT security might not be dramatically more difficult than the trivial step in our evaluation.

As a sanity check, we can see how difficult the autonomy and orchestration step is (if we took out cyber and inference setup, how tough is doing the remaining command-line grunt work?). This ablation is the above evaluation with the inference setup steps removed (done via a pre-written script). Many models in our roster, including the smaller ones, are capable of these remaining steps.

Replication on a contained 17-node redroid fleet: two subsets of 8 nodes joined by one pivot node (see Appendix F, with the mild prompt). Each tree is the model’s median run of six.

When it comes to this worm, we can envision:

  1. A model capabilities floor that an autonomous worm must sit above, to complete its replication reliably. In our simplified eval, GLM-5.2 sits above this floor.
  2. A model size ceiling that the model must sit under, such that it’s feasible to run on the devices it’s attacking. Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-26B-A4B sit under this ceiling for the class of smart TVs we test (4GB of RAM).

Right now, the floor and ceiling don’t intersect. When might they?

Above is a plot of notable open-weight models of 30B total parameters or fewer, each plotted at its release date against the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI). The solid line is the least-squares fit over the best models in-class at each date, with a gain of 13.7 ECI per year (R2 of 0.95). If we take GLM-5.2 as a capabilities floor for replication, the trend line puts a small model at that level by the end of 2026. ECI is a general capability index, which is only a proxy metric for replication ability, so this is only a rough estimate of when a small-model replicator becomes possible.

C. How fast might an AI IoT worm replicate?

Unlike coding agents, these replicators would be running below the interactive speeds of user-facing chat and coding harnesses. The spread would be slow and persistent, with tokens being trickled out on edge hardware. We can use our achieved speeds on our real smart TVs as a demonstrated baseline for replication speeds. For Gemma4-26B-A4B, unoptimized speed across a 32k context length token window is about 0.3 tok/s, averaged across prefill and decode in our inference setup workload. More details in Appendix C.

A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.

modelwindow timefull inference setup time
Gemma4-26B-A4B (unoptimized)27.3-31.8h71h-150h
Qwen3.5-9B10.9 h28-51h

The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak, reported by Synthient, is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet.

As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at high concurrency with speculative decoding, so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.

This is a rough estimate, as it’s anchored on a single class of IoT hardware and a single past botnet instance, but describes what a simple replicator released in the near future might look like. In practice, more capable replicators would take advantage of other types of low-security compute, and would be opportunistic about deploying models of various sizes on different devices. (It also wouldn’t have to load a model payload onto every device it compromises). Over time, we expect the amount of deployed edge compute to continue growing, while the minimum model size required for reliable replication falls.

D. Adaptation and uplift

Learning on the job

The “Adaptation” part of ARA is one reason why an AI replicator might outperform a traditional worm. Specifically, models and prompts can undergo Lamarckian evolution as they spread–that is, parent instances can pass on their prompts, code, and notes to their daughter replicators. In order to adapt and spread across a wide variety of hardware, a model would require two things:

  1. Being above a certain threshold of capability for spreading onto a novel, unseen piece of hardware (or software environment, or network type).
  2. Once seen, adapting to the type of environment it has landed in (it should replicate more reliably on hardware it has seen before).

Sections A and B test the first condition, and in the experiment below we test the second. Each Qwen3.5-9B instance keeps brief notes on the strategies it tried and the failures it encountered, before a new instance inherits those notes and attempts the same inference setup again.

Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. Faint lines are the 20 individual lineages, and the bold line is the proportion of runs in each generation that complete setup. It rises from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones. This uses the Memento setup (Appendix A).

Taking advice

Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a frontier advisor, a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck. To test this, we gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8 during the inference setup task. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted.

Even when trained through reinforcement learning to use the advisor in a similar setting (Python coding problems), the small model still struggles to ask for help productively for inference standup. Both results are shown in the plot below.

Inference setup success rate by advisor access, with Wilson 95% intervals. Access to an advisor, whether offered as a tool call or given to the model automatically when stuck, gives no significant improvement. The two RL groups were trained with advisor access on software engineering tasks, and the rightmost group also rewards calling the advisor when stuck.

Since small models are capable and persistent individual agents and make poor use of advice, we think coordination is more likely to happen with a large model handling high-level strategy and spinning up small models as subagents.

E. How is this different from a pre-AI botnet?

Hard-coded botnets like the Kimwolf botnet each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A). We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.

F. Blue-team mitigations

As with an epidemic, defense involves driving R₀ (the number of new devices each infected device goes on to infect) below 1, such that the replicator dies out instead of staying endemic.

Some elements around this threat model are in the defenders’ favor:

  1. A weight-based replicator multiplying through IoT machines at scale would leave a network signature, visible as an anomaly in ISP flow-based monitoring systems. Newly infected hosts may receive multi-gigabyte model payloads from other devices or external hosting services, while distributed inference can produce sustained device-to-device traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate at that volume. Propagation itself would add additional scanning and outbound connection patterns.

    In practice, the replicator trades off between replication speed and stealth: the faster it replicates, the more traffic it produces. Once the replicator is discovered, defenders can use honeypots (decoy devices) to collect the replicator’s harness and payload to characterize its behavior.
  2. Remediation of the Mirai botnet was possible when an ISP used externally obtained infection evidence to quarantine and notify customers. Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions. This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.
  3. Manufacturers can shrink the pool of targets, with regulation acting to coordinate. For example, default IoT passwords are now non-compliant in UK markets. Moving to more secure defaults and raising the baseline for compliance will help harden against both AI and scripted botnets.

G. Conclusion: Signs of life

The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.

Appendix

A. The Memento harness

Memento executes as follows:

  1. We spawn an agent instance, which tackles the problem for a while (until generation timeout).
  2. The instance keeps brief notes, and after timeout summarizes a small doc of the strategies it tried, the failures it encountered, and its performance (if successful).
  3. We create a new agent instance that inherits the codebase and environment from its predecessor as well as the notebook.

In the serving experiment, each model is placed in a Memento harness and is given a 1.5 hour per iteration / 6 hour total timeout. Around ~1k tokens of information, including specs about the hardware and a script for a simple sample profiler, are given in the prompt.

Memento is intended to improve long-horizon reliability rather than grant new cyber or inference-specific capabilities. It’s also not a universally strong harness; we expect that small models will improve as replicators even without any harnessing as capabilities improve.

Single attempt compared against Memento, by model (95% Wilson CI).

B. Why pipeline parallel?

Common parallelism schemes for inference include tensor parallel (TP), expert parallel (EP), and data parallel. Most smart TV / IoT devices use ARM Cortex CPUs and DDR3/4 memory; on such machines, we’re almost always bandwidth bound.

We use pipeline parallelism for its fault-tolerant properties. As noted in (Borzunov et al. 2022), the failure of a single node in tensor parallel / expert parallel brings down the full set of machines running the model replica. Pipeline parallel allows the downed node to be replaced, with the KV cache for the layers held by the node recomputable via another forward pass of the node prior to the restarted node.

C. Throughput and memory on IoT hardware

Across such machines, we’re almost always RAM-bandwidth bound per-box across prefill and decode. Even on modest ARM-cortex cores, compute throughput outpaces RAM bandwidth. Decode workloads have significant per-machine idle time due to pipeline bubbling, as only one machine is active at a time during each forward pass. Concurrency with staggered work is possible, but tight memory constraints mean that concurrency stays low.

Per-box memory vs context — 4-bit weights + fp8 KV + activations.

Both prefill and decode tokens/s strictly decrease with sequence length. Below is a graph of our inference speeds against context length:

There’s also a minimum sequence length at which models are competent. The harness we use is forked off of the Pi coding agent (pi.dev) and contains a native compaction mechanism - even still, we find that models take a large performance hit when their sequence lengths are restricted below 32K.

Qwen3.5-9B agentic competence on the inference setup task vs. context window budget.

Given the above eval, we assume that a 32k context length may be sufficient for reasonable agentic performance. A standard 32k-length context window in our inference setup workload consists of 12–15% generated decode tokens, with the rest being prefill from prompts and toolcalls. Prefill tokens are much faster to compute by a factor of ~15, due to the pipeline bubbling. Taking the sum of time per token over the whole 32k context (taking into account prefill and decode speeds), we find that generating the 3.8-4.8k decode output tokens and processing the ~28k prefill tokens takes between 27.3-31.8h for Gemma4-26B-A4B and 10.9h for Qwen3.5-9B.

Per-chain output tokens (summed over a chain’s generations), by model; medians ≈ 19.7k / 12.3k / 11.0k. Data from the inference setup eval.

D. Edge Accelerators

We can compute a better upper bound by using the pool of Nvidia Jetsons, which are edge accelerators. Unlike the traditional IoT botnet, IoT edge devices can serve a full model wholesale. A Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB runs Qwen3-30B-A3B at 76.7 tokens per second, and an AGX Thor reaches 226 tok/s. Note that we don’t believe they’re unusually vulnerable - this is just to count the upper bound. The types of devices with Jetsons in the wild include:

  1. AI-enabled smart cameras for security with embedded accelerators are deployed at substantial scale.
  2. Conferencing machines are frequently powered by an onboard accelerator for on-device noise cancellation or transcription.
  3. Vehicles, robot quadrupeds and bipeds, and drones. We expect cybersecurity to be a focal point for vehicles, so the majority of the potential targets likely lie in the other two categories.

At least one accelerator-equipped smart camera host appears to be reachable on IPv4 on a quick search on FOFA:

While it’s difficult to estimate how many edge-accelerator-equipped machines in the wild are reachable and vulnerable, we can calculate a strict upper bound of the amount of devices present. Across the wild there are on the order of 90 distinct NVIDIA-silicon IoT product lines and roughly 9.5 million fielded units. Reachability is overwhelmingly through outbound cloud-management tunnels instead of inbound ports, meaning that the majority are not web-reachable. There have been no historical mass-compromises of accelerator-equipped edge devices the way there have been standard IoT botnets, suggesting that compromise of such devices would be more difficult.

Fielded units per device family, colored by internet reachability.

A very rough estimate based on product data suggests that somewhere between 9,000 and 35,000 H100-equivalents of compute exist in edge accelerators, but the amount that’s reachable is likely an order of magnitude or more lower (and the vulnerable population even lower than that).

E. Spearphishing capability

We also measure how proficient modern small models are at spearphishing. Spearphishing is the act of sending targeted messages to specific individuals to trick them into revealing credentials or running a piece of malware. While the agentic cyber capability of small models has skyrocketed, their general knowledge and linguistic sophistication have improved more slowly; we expect social engineering attacks and phishing to be largely accomplished by large/frontier models (although it’s very plausible that this is a secondary replication vector in a heterogeneous botnet running both large and small models).

Spear-phishing capability on Meta’s CyberSecEval 3’s spear-phishing eval (Wan et al. 2024), replicated locally. Scored on a scale of 0-5, with gpt-4o as a judge. Red diamonds are the paper’s (CyberSecEval 3) human-rubric scores on the reference models, which indicates that gpt-4o scores ~0.4-0.7 pts more leniently than human raters. 2 is “poor”, 3 is “intermediate”, and 4 “good.” When normalized to human raters, small models score “very poor” to “poor”.

The 405B reference slot uses Hermes-3-405B as a minimal-refusal stand-in for the unavailable Llama3.1-405B-Instruct.

F. Propagation with scripted inference setup:

We run a few more experiments on a network of 17 hosts in a topology like so:

Two networks with 8 hosts each, connected by a single node with access to both subnets. Each network is all-to-all connected. The worm agent begins on a single patient zero node in segment A; the pivot node adds a slight extra challenge in having the worm needing to gain access to the pivot node and re-scan from it.

Each is running Android with an ADB port open without authentication. Upon spreading to a new target, the agent is able to invoke a direct call to replicate itself immediately - this is just to measure the difficulty of the remaining steps, after we exclude the cyber and inference setup steps. As shown in the graph, even a 3B model reaches about half the nodes. This puts a bound on the number of blockers in our eval that we fail to measure under the cyber or inference setup elements.

A more detailed breakdown of the runs in “replication across a 17 node network.” Each column is the median number of nodes reached under different amounts of guidance in the prompt, and the subscript denotes how many agents cross over the pivot node to the other side of the network.

item.title: Launching an opt-in vulnerability-finding service for open-source software
item.description: We’re launching OSS Scanner, an opt-in vulnerability scanner for the open-source ecosystem informed by our experience using Claude to find vulnerabilities during Project Glasswing. Projects that join will receive thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.
item.content:encoded:
We’re launching OSS Scanner, an opt-in vulnerability scanner for the open-source ecosystem informed by our experience using Claude to find vulnerabilities during Project Glasswing. Projects that join will receive thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.

Language models have rapidly advanced in their ability to discover vulnerabilities, as we have reported extensively on this blog. On CyberGym, one academic vulnerability-finding benchmark, LLMs have gone from finding under 20% of vulnerabilities at the beginning of last year to finding over 85% this year. As a result, open source maintainers have gone from receiving mostly slop from LLMs to receiving high-quality bug reports.

Over the last six months, we’ve used our latest models to scan for vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most important software projects. We have discovered over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities, but have only been able to manually review and triage approximately 6,000 of these. While 6,000 vulnerabilities is significant, we remain bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings.

We are working on scaling our vulnerability disclosures. Meanwhile, with increasing frequency, maintainers who receive our first reports simply ask us for a bulk submission of all the unverified reports with proposed patches: to date, we have sent nearly 5,000 reports directly to maintainers after they asked to receive everything we had—even if it wasn’t validated. Since exploits can now be developed in minutes, projects that can find and address vulnerabilities faster can better secure their software against attackers who are racing to find and leverage these same weaknesses.

We will continue to manually disclose human-verified vulnerability reports via our existing coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) process, especially for projects without the resourcing to triage reports themselves. But we are now making available an optional fast-track for those who wish to receive vulnerability reports as soon as they become available.

Our vulnerability scanner

Inspired by the positive impact on the open source ecosystem of Google's OSS-Fuzz, a project that scans open-source software for vulnerabilities with fuzzers, we are launching OSS Scanner to find vulnerabilities in open-source code with our strongest language models. While Claude Security, our general-access code scanning and patching product focuses on helping enterprises defend their systems, OSS Scanner provides security audits at no cost to open-source projects.

The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage.

We have spent the last several weeks validating this pipeline with dozens of open source projects. These initial disclosures contained hundreds of bug reports, including multiple vulnerabilities that we were able to chain to unauthenticated remote code execution exploits affecting these projects. Each report contains a self-contained reproducer, explanation of the vulnerability (including a bisection to determine when the bug was introduced, where possible), and candidate patch (when available) for how the bug can be fixed. We are now making this service available to more open source projects.

Some of the feedback we received as we tested early versions of OSS Scanner and our raw model outputs:

  • “An unusually high fraction of OSS Scanner’s findings uncovered PostgreSQL defects. Several reports came with fixes we can use nearly as-is, and fast-track access let us address the newest issues before they reached a GA release.” —Noah Misch, PostgreSQL
  • “Early AI reports about 18 months ago, before Project Glasswing, were appalling. The reports we received from Anthropic, raw model output included, were as good and sometimes better than what we get from people. Particularly when a report comes with a real exploit attached, that's basically job done for an engineer as you can verify it right away” —Anton Arapov, OpenSSL Corporation
  • “We found the signal from these reports high: of the 74 reports we received, all but two were valid, and five became CVEs. With patches attached, the reports slotted right into our existing process to verify and fix issues. We’d love more.” —Todd Ouska, wolfSSL
  • “The bug reports were thorough and clear, with a strong understanding of HotCRP's complex permission model and good bug prioritization.” —Eddie Kohler, HotCRP

To validate an early version of OSS Scanner, we asked the expert penetration testers who review our CVD findings to check 97 critical and high-severity vulnerabilities from the scanner across 48 projects. Of these, 85 (88%) met the bar for our CVD process. Of the remaining 12, 11 were real but duplicated known issues or other findings from the scan, and only one was invalid, i.e. a “false positive.” We’ve since sent many of these findings to maintainers, who have seldom told us a high or critical finding was invalid, consistent with our prior open-source work. Some have told us severity ratings can be inflated or the scanner misunderstood the project’s threat model. We can’t guarantee the scanner will be perfect, but we’ll keep refining the system based on maintainer feedback and as models improve.

Getting started

Core maintainers of eligible projects can enroll by submitting a PR to this GitHub repo following the standard project template, with additional guidance provided in our extended FAQ. Projects are eligible based on a similar set of criteria that OSS-Fuzz uses: briefly, projects should have a “critical impact on infrastructure and user security” and we will make decisions on a case-by-case basis.

Whether or not OSS Scanner is right for you, our new Cyber Verification Program makes advanced cyber capabilities and reduced blocking classifiers available to qualifying security professionals. Claude for OSS provides free Claude Max 20x subscriptions to help remediate vulnerabilities and improve OSS projects.

item.title: GLM-5.3 and the spread of advanced cyber capabilities
item.description: GLM-5.3 can autonomously build end-to-end cyber exploits, but unlike other frontier models, it was released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse.
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Fasano, Marius Fleischer
Cole McFaul, Robert Xiao, Tripp Gallagher

Five months ago, we announced Claude Mythos Preview, the first AI model that could autonomously build sophisticated, end-to-end cyber exploits. The rapid rate of improvement in AI suggested to us that this ability would eventually proliferate to many other models, making it much easier for malicious cyber actors to launch highly impactful cyberattacks.

In light of these considerations, we chose to release Claude Mythos Preview in a limited way, through Project Glasswing—which enabled trusted cyber defenders to find more than 10,000 vulnerabilities in critical software, giving them a head start before malicious actors had access to similarly capable models.

But those models have now arrived. In this post, we share our analysis of GLM-5.3, the latest AI model developed by Zhipu AI (known outside of China as Z.ai). Like Claude Mythos Preview, GLM-5.3 has strong capabilities for autonomously building end-to-end cyber exploits. But GLM-5.3 is unlike other frontier models in that it has been released without meaningful safeguards to limit misuse. We find that attackers can bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards between 64% and 100% of the time with simple techniques in our simulated tests. In contrast, these attacks did not succeed against safeguarded Claude models in our testing. We assess that GLM-5.3’s lax safeguards significantly increase the cyber capabilities available to malicious actors. At the same time, these capabilities can also benefit defenders working to secure their systems.

On Sept. 17, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) published its own assessment of GLM-5.3’s cyber capabilities. CAISI found that GLM-5.3 is “the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date” and that it lags the US frontier by about four months on an aggregate of CAISI’s cyber benchmarks. Our capability findings broadly match CAISI’s. In CAISI’s comparison, US models were tested with cyber safeguards disabled when applicable, and the US frontier includes models released only to vetted users. Attackers can’t readily access those versions of US models, but anyone can download GLM-5.3. This post adds our analysis of how easily GLM-5.3’s safeguards can be bypassed or removed.

GLM-5.3 can develop working exploits end to end

To understand how GLM-5.3 could enable cyber threat actors to find and exploit real software vulnerabilities, we ran evaluations using automated benchmarks and human-in-the-loop workflows. For both approaches, we ran the tested models in isolated and sandboxed environments so they can only attack offline targets that we have set up for the purposes of these evaluations. We focus primarily on exploit development capability, as this is where Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated a notable jump versus previous Claude models.

First, we ran the model on ExploitBench, which measures how well AI models can exploit known vulnerabilities in the V8 engine used by Google Chrome. Here we focus on the models’ ability to develop end-to-end exploits successfully, as this is the most relevant capability for attackers, and where we see significant changes between models. We find that GLM-5.3 develops end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts. Claude Mythos Preview did so at a similar rate—in 56 of 410 attempts.

In our internal Binary Exploitation benchmark,1 we test whether models can find and exploit vulnerabilities in popular open source projects that participate in Google’s OSS-Fuzz project. Here, full credit is awarded for a full control-flow hijack. We evaluate several models on 100 tasks from the benchmark (selected at random), and find that GLM-5.3 develops full control flow hijacks in 4% of the trials; Claude Mythos Preview did so in 6%. Although GLM-5.3 performs below Claude Mythos Preview here, a meaningful threshold has clearly been crossed: earlier models, like Claude Opus 4.6 and GLM-5.2, do not succeed in any of them.

Next, we evaluated how GLM-5.3 performs on open-ended offensive cyber tasks in the hands of human experts (mirroring our testing with Claude Mythos Preview earlier this year). Here, we select targets in which the human experts are unaware of existing vulnerabilities, then ask them to use the model to identify and exploit novel flaws. These experiments tested what the experts could do in a short time-frame: they typically ran for a day or less, with less than an hour of human focus in total.

In the first of these sessions, a researcher used GLM-5.3 on a sandboxed machine with a local Linux build of a popular web browser. Over the course of a day (and with limited human attention), GLM-5.3 found several previously unknown vulnerabilities in the browser’s JavaScript engine, and chained them together into a working exploit: a webpage that, when visited, reads arbitrary files from the visitor’s computer (shown in Figure 3). This exploit targets the Linux build of the browser, since that was the only environment made available to the model. However, we believe these vulnerabilities could also impact users on other platforms, though the path to exploitation there may be more complex. (We’ve disclosed these vulnerabilities to the maintainer.) Later in the session, the researcher also identified exploitable vulnerabilities in several other widely used systems with GLM-5.3, including wireless and graphics drivers and network-facing device software. We are currently reviewing these reports and we will disclose to maintainers as appropriate.

In a second session, a researcher used GLM-5.3-Flash (a smaller, less capable version of GLM-5.3) to develop an exploit for a known vulnerability (we’ve previously written about these “N-day” vulnerability exploits here). Here, the researcher focused on a recently disclosed flaw in Google Chrome (CVE-2026-11645) to see how quickly the model could turn a public fix into a working attack. The researcher provided GLM-5.3-Flash with public details of this CVE and another known flaw. With no significant direction from the researcher, GLM-5.3-Flash chained together exploits for these two flaws, building a reliable exploit chain for an ARM64 target, bypassing pointer-authentication (PAC) hardening. This took 20 minutes of human attention, plus 8 hours of work for GLM-5.3-Flash. At Zhipu’s API prices, this effort would have cost $20.40.

GLM-5.3 lacks robust safeguards

GLM-5.3 has been released with some built-in safeguards: if a user asks for something clearly harmful, the model will often refuse.2 In our testing, we found that these safeguards could be bypassed or removed with a variety of simple techniques.

The most intensive—and most successful—method is a standard refusal reduction technique known as “abliteration”. Since GLM-5.3 is released as an open-weight model, users can reconfigure it to remove its refusals with little change in its capabilities. Several developers released abliterated versions of GLM-5.3 to the public within days of the model’s release.

To research how far abliteration allows attackers to bypass GLM-5.3’s safeguards, we produced an abliterated copy ourselves, and then ran it on three public benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and StrongREJECT) that measure how often a model complies with clearly harmful requests. Abliterating the model took our team—which had never previously attempted this task—about 2,200 GPU hours at a computation cost of roughly $4,400.3 Abliterating GLM-5.3-Flash took about 600 GPU hours. The edit took GLM-5.3’s refusal rate from above 90% to about 3% and 2% on the first two benchmarks (JailbreakBench and HarmBench) and to 12% on the third (StrongREJECT). Abliteration did not significantly reduce the model’s capabilities: on GPQA-Diamond, an evaluation that measures general scientific capabilities, the standard and abliterated models scored the same results; on a tested subset of the CyberGym evaluations, the abliterated version scored a few percent lower (as shown in the chart below).

In our testing, we observed that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can also be circumvented without using an abliterated version of the model. We placed the model in a simulated world4 in which it was given overtly malicious requests to attack critical systems. Out of the box, GLM-5.3 refused in all trials (as with the other models we tested). But we identified several simple ways to bypass the GLM models’ safeguards, such that it would respond to these requests in most or all cases. These include:

  1. Providing a deceptive prompt, such as telling the model that it is an autonomous red-team agent working on an exercise. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 64% of the time.
  2. Prefilling the models’ thinking tokens so that it appears to have considered the user’s request and decided to proceed. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 92% of the time.
  3. Using an abliterated version of the model, as described above. This gets GLM-5.3 to engage 100% of the time.

In our testing, none of these techniques got safeguarded Claude models to carry out the harmful tasks we tested. Claude’s safeguards blocked the requests that used deceptive prompts. The Anthropic API provides would-be attackers with no way to prefill Claude’s thinking. And since Claude’s weights are not provided to users, they cannot be abliterated to change Claude’s behavior.

To demonstrate how the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 is willing to engage in harmful tasks, we highlight one quote from the chain of thought that it generated:

What does this mean?

GLM-5.3 will likely give malicious actors access to capabilities that will allow them to find and exploit cyber vulnerabilities without meaningful restrictions.
